summary.headline: No schema.org markup anywhere -- Open Graph and Twitter Card are excellent site-wide, but nothing exists in the deeper vocabulary — high severity, Add an Organization JSON-LD node (name, url, logo, sameAs) site-wide, JobPosting markup on individual career listings, and Article markup (headline, datePublished, author) on blog and changelog entries -- alongside the existing Open Graph tags, not instead of them.

findings.title: No schema.org markup anywhere -- Open Graph and Twitter Card are excellent site-wide, but nothing exists in the deeper vocabulary
findings.evidence: 0 of 15 sampled pages contain JSON-LD, microdata, or RDFa in any form, including /about (organization identity), /careers/* (job listing), and /blog/* and /changelog/* (editorial/dated content) -- all pages whose detected patterns license Organization, JobPosting or Article markup respectively. This is not a general machine-readability gap: every one of the same 15 pages carries complete, well-formed Open Graph (title, description, image) and Twitter Card (card, site, title, description, creator, image) tags. The site has clearly invested in the lower-depth preview channel and not at all in the deeper, more structured one -- Open Graph carries a title/description/image triple but no address, no job-posting fields, no article author or date, none of which OG's vocabulary supports.

reproduction.expected: >= 1, containing an Organization node with sameAs, and a JobPosting node on the careers page

suggested_action.summary: Add an Organization JSON-LD node (name, url, logo, sameAs) site-wide, JobPosting markup on individual career listings, and Article markup (headline, datePublished, author) on blog and changelog entries -- alongside the existing Open Graph tags, not instead of them.
suggested_action.mechanism: Open Graph and schema.org solve different problems: OG tells a link-preview generator what thumbnail and one-line description to show; schema.org tells a system extracting structured facts what an Organization's identity anchors are, what a job posting's requirements and location are, or when an article was published. The site already has every value these blocks need -- the same title, description and image already populate the OG tags -- so this is markup generation from existing data, not new content work.
steps: Add a single Organization JSON-LD block (name, url, logo, sameAs to the X/LinkedIn profiles already linked in the page footer) to the shared template.
Add JobPosting JSON-LD to the careers listing template, sourced from the same data already rendered on the page.
Add Article JSON-LD (headline, datePublished, author) to blog and changelog templates.

findings.title: Dated content uses the <time> element inconsistently -- present but missing its datetime attribute on the blog, absent entirely on the changelog
findings.evidence: The blog post at /blog/designing-remote-work-at-linear renders its publish date inside a <time> element twice ('October 29, 2025'), but neither instance carries a datetime attribute -- the semantically-correct tag is used as a plain styling wrapper rather than as machine-readable markup; a parser looking specifically for <time datetime="..."> (a common, standard extraction pattern) gets nothing. The changelog entry at /changelog/2019-06-20-international-keyboard-shortcut-improvements carries no <time> element at all, despite the entry's own URL encoding its date. A cross-reference link to that same entry elsewhere on the page displays it as 'June 21, 2019' -- one day off from the URL's '2019-06-20' -- a minor but real internal inconsistency in how the same date is stored versus displayed.

reproduction.observed: <time> tags with no datetime attribute on the blog; zero <time> tags on the changelog entry
reproduction.expected: <time datetime="2025-10-29">October 29, 2025</time> -- the same visible text, with the machine-readable attribute added

suggested_action.summary: Add a datetime attribute to the existing <time> elements on blog posts, and add a <time datetime="..."> element to changelog entries using the date already encoded in each entry's own URL slug.
suggested_action.mechanism: The publish date is not missing data -- it already renders correctly as visible text and is already encoded in the changelog's own URL structure -- so this is a template fix, not a content or data-sourcing problem. Populating the datetime attribute from the same value already used to generate the visible text and the URL slug also removes the one-day discrepancy observed between the two.
steps: Add datetime="<ISO date>" to the blog post template's existing <time> elements.
Add a <time datetime="..."> element to the changelog entry template, sourced from the same date used to build the URL slug.
suggested_action.verification: curl -s <any dated URL> | grep -o '<time[^>]*datetime="[^"]*"' returns a match.

opportunities.title: Add HowTo or Article schema specifically to the /docs and /enablement/guides content
opportunities.rationale: These pages are clearly structured, step-oriented reference content -- exactly the kind of material an assistant answering a 'how do I do X in Linear' question would want to quote directly and attribute precisely, distinct from the general Organization/Article markup already recommended for the rest of the site.
opportunities.mechanism: Type-specific markup on the pages most likely to be cited for direct how-to questions gives an assistant a more precise attribution unit than a generic Article type would.
steps: Add HowTo or TechArticle JSON-LD to the docs and enablement-guide templates specifically, ahead of a broader site-wide rollout.

not_assessed.check: Off-site corroboration and entity ambiguity (freshness-corroboration-audit, checks 4-5)
not_assessed.reason: Not performed in this run to stay within the demonstration's time budget.
not_assessed.impact: Not a meaningful concern for a well-known, distinctively-named entity, but genuinely not checked.

not_assessed.reason: 15 of 1,009 discovered candidates across 69 templates were sampled -- a broad, stratified cross-section (docs, blog, changelog, careers, customers, guides), not an exhaustive audit of every template.
not_assessed.impact: Findings should be read as representative of the shared page templates observed, not as claims about every individual page on the site.
